{"artifact":"SmeDossierEnvelope","schema_version":"0.4.0","stage_id":"02.dossier_sections","probe":"rdmv-nj-d","lineage":{"input_manifest_sha256":"2b586ec98b5ef40a951634082a02acb8b716869cccc92439fa079518e2f1600b","candidate_lineage_id":"2026-10-28-rdmv-nj-class-d:lineage:14","source_registry_sha256":"057b72c7c679c997f56ae00ef97a6b14dbe264551f4121b9bf67b0457d9cf7c1","source_liveness_sha256":"1ca7bfbb9e3c0a6b19e5e808ecab6fe8329f3b4799e394abc260d65c1d6513e7"},"envelope_scope":{"kind":"partial_chunk","assigned_section_ids":["C"],"chunk_index":1,"chunk_total":1},"section_char_limit":12000,"sections":[{"section_id":"C","chunk_id":"C.01","merge_seq":1,"domain":"Driver responsibility: occupant protection, vehicle condition and getting started","heading":"C — Driver responsibility: seat belts, child passenger rules, air bags, vehicle condition, snow and ice, carbon monoxide, starting the car and idling","learner_facing":true,"markdown":"## C — Driver responsibility: seat belts, child passenger rules, air bags, vehicle condition, snow and ice, carbon monoxide, starting the car and idling
Knowledge domain: what a New Jersey driver owes every occupant and every other road user before and during a trip — the seat belt law and its exemptions, the child passenger safety law, air bag safety, basic vehicle condition checks, snow and ice removal, carbon monoxide hazards, the pre-drive checklist, mirror setup and the idling limit.

FACT_ID: sec04-F01 | anchor: A01
New Jersey law requires the driver and every passenger of a passenger vehicle, such as a car, van, pickup truck or SUV, to wear a seat belt. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0042]

FACT_ID: sec04-F02 | anchor: A01
An unbelted driver, front-seat passenger or child under 18 is a primary offense, so a police officer may stop the vehicle for that violation alone. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0042]

FACT_ID: sec04-F03 | anchor: A01
The driver is answerable for every passenger under age 18, while front-seat passengers aged 18 or older are answerable for themselves. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0042]

FACT_ID: sec04-F04 | anchor: A01
Unbuckled back-seat riders aged 18 or older can receive a summons under a secondary law, but only when the vehicle has been stopped for some other reason. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0042]

FACT_ID: sec04-F05 | anchor: A01
A driver holding a GDL permit or probationary license must wear a seat belt and must also make every passenger, in any seat, buckle up. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0042]

FACT_ID: sec04-F06 | anchor: A01
The seat belt law exempts passenger vehicles built before July 1, 1966, vehicles that federal law does not require to have belts, and people with a physical or medical reason confirmed in writing by a licensed physician. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0042]

FACT_ID: sec04-F07 | anchor: A01
Wearing a seat belt improves a motorist's chance of surviving a crash by 60 percent. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0042]

FACT_ID: sec04-F08 | anchor: A02
Hitting the dashboard or windshield at 30 mph is compared with falling from the top of a three-story building. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0043]

FACT_ID: sec04-F09 | anchor: A02
The lap belt should sit under the abdomen and low on the hips, and the shoulder belt should cross the collarbone and breastbone while staying away from the neck. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0043]

FACT_ID: sec04-F10 | anchor: A02
Because air bags are only supplemental protection, both the lap and shoulder belts should be worn on every trip and in every seat, back seat included. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0043]

FACT_ID: sec04-F11 | anchor: A02
Every child restraint system made since January 1, 1981, must be designed to pass demanding safety tests and carries a label giving its manufacture date and its conformity with federal safety standards. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0043]

FACT_ID: sec04-F12 | anchor: A02
An infant seat must never be turned to face forward, and the seat label shows the child size and weight it is designed to protect. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0043]

FACT_ID: sec04-F13 | anchor: A03
Children under age eight and shorter than 57 inches (4 feet, 9 inches) must ride in a rear seat, either in a forward-facing restraint with a five-point harness until they outgrow it and then a booster seat, or in a booster seat. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0044]

FACT_ID: sec04-F14 | anchor: A03
Children under age four who weigh under 40 pounds must ride in a rear seat in a five-point-harness restraint, either rear-facing until they outgrow the maker's limits and then forward-facing, or forward-facing. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0044]

FACT_ID: sec04-F15 | anchor: A03
The manual says children under age two and those weighing under 30 pounds must ride in a rear-facing child restraint equipped with a five-point harness. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0044]

FACT_ID: sec04-F16 | anchor: A03
Using the car seat on every ride and using it correctly each time, following the seat's own instructions, is the best protection a driver can give a child. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0044]

FACT_ID: sec04-F17 | anchor: A04
All children under age eight must sit in a rear seat, and only a vehicle with no rear seat allows them to ride in an approved restraint or booster seat up front. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0045]

FACT_ID: sec04-F18 | anchor: A04
A rear-facing child restraint may never be placed in a front seat that has a passenger-side air bag that has not been disabled or turned off. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0045]

FACT_ID: sec04-F19 | anchor: A04
Violating the child passenger safety law can bring a fine of $50 to $75, plus fees and court costs. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0045]

FACT_ID: sec04-F20 | anchor: A04
Air bags are meant to add to seat belt protection in frontal crashes, and federal standards require them in all new passenger cars and light trucks. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0045]

FACT_ID: sec04-F21 | anchor: A04
Air bags can inflate at speeds up to 200 mph, and a correctly belted adult of average size usually reaches the bag only after it is fully inflated. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0045]

FACT_ID: sec04-F22 | anchor: A04
Air bags have saved many belted adults but could seriously injure or kill children sitting in the front seat. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0045]

FACT_ID: sec04-F23 | anchor: A05
Children 12 years old and younger should always ride in the back seat. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0046]

FACT_ID: sec04-F24 | anchor: A05
A vehicle has an air bag when the steering wheel and dashboard panel show the words air bag or the letters SRS or SIR. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0046]

FACT_ID: sec04-F25 | anchor: A06
Backup lights should come on when reversing, and New Jersey law forbids having any backup light on while the vehicle is moving forward. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0047]

FACT_ID: sec04-F26 | anchor: A06
Brakes need checking if the vehicle pulls to one side when stopping, the pedal feels taut, or there is unusual squealing or grinding. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0047]

FACT_ID: sec04-F27 | anchor: A06
After driving through water, gently pump conventional disc and drum brakes to test and dry them, since braking hard could lock them up. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0047]

FACT_ID: sec04-F28 | anchor: A06
A vehicle should be able to stop within 25 feet from 20 mph, which a driver can test in an empty parking lot using chalk marks. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0047]

FACT_ID: sec04-F29 | anchor: A06
Anti-lock brakes are tested with steady pressure on the pedal, and a driver should never pump ABS brakes or jerk the steering wheel while braking. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0047]

FACT_ID: sec04-F30 | anchor: A07
Sound the horn to signal that you are passing, to announce yourself as you leave a blind alley, curve or driveway, or to warn another driver of danger, but do not overuse it. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0048]

FACT_ID: sec04-F31 | anchor: A07
Check tire pressure often, especially while the tires are cold, using the pressure listed in the owner's manual or on the driver's door jamb. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0048]

FACT_ID: sec04-F32 | anchor: A07
Do not drive on tires with less than 1/16 inch of tread, roughly the edge of a penny, and do not mix radials with other tire types. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0048]

FACT_ID: sec04-F33 | anchor: A08
New Jersey prohibits add-on tinting on the windshield and the front side windows. [A08]
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0049]

FACT_ID: sec04-F34 | anchor: A08
Before driving, a motorist must make every reasonable effort to clear built-up snow and ice from the exposed surfaces of the vehicle, including the hood, trunk, roof and windshield. [A08]
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0049]

FACT_ID: sec04-F35 | anchor: A08
Not clearing snow or ice brings a fine of $25 to $75 even if none falls off, and fines up to $1,500 when falling snow or ice causes injury or property damage. [A08]
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0049]

FACT_ID: sec04-F36 | anchor: A08
Carbon monoxide is an odorless, colorless gas in vehicle exhaust that can build up to deadly levels in or around a vehicle. [A08]
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0049]

FACT_ID: sec04-F37 | anchor: A09
Carbon monoxide can kill before a person notices any symptom such as headache, dizziness, nausea, chest pain, confusion or loss of consciousness. [A09]
Source: [A09 -> pdf-0050]

FACT_ID: sec04-F38 | anchor: A09
If carbon monoxide poisoning is suspected, move the person away from the source and call 911; in a vehicle, switch off the engine and get out as soon as it is safe. [A09]
Source: [A09 -> pdf-0050]

FACT_ID: sec04-F39 | anchor: A09
Before getting into the vehicle, look both in front of it and behind it, because children or objects may be hidden in spots the driver cannot see from the seat. [A09]
Source: [A09 -> pdf-0050]

FACT_ID: sec04-F40 | anchor: A10
Before moving off, the seat should let you reach every pedal and control (about an arm's length from the wheel for most drivers), the mirrors should be adjusted, belts fastened, the gear in park or neutral with the parking brake set, and the doors locked. [A10]
Source: [A10 -> pdf-0051]

FACT_ID: sec04-F41 | anchor: A10
More than 95 percent of the information a driver needs comes through vision. [A10]
Source: [A10 -> pdf-0051]

FACT_ID: sec04-F42 | anchor: A11
A motorist should have an eye examination every two years. [A11]
Source: [A11 -> pdf-0052]

FACT_ID: sec04-F43 | anchor: A11
Set the outside mirror so the tip of the driver-side front door handle appears in the lower right of the mirror. [A11]
Source: [A11 -> pdf-0052]

FACT_ID: sec04-F44 | anchor: A11
After starting the engine, turn and look back to confirm the path is clear rather than relying on the rearview mirrors, and watch for pedestrians, bicycles and mopeds. [A11]
Source: [A11 -> pdf-0052]

FACT_ID: sec04-F45 | anchor: A11
New Jersey requires every motorist to keep vehicle idling to three minutes or less. [A11]
Source: [A11 -> pdf-0052]

FACT_ID: sec04-F46 | anchor: A11
Vehicle and property owners face fines of $250 to $1,000 for each idling violation. [A11]
Source: [A11 -> pdf-0052]

Misconceptions: air bags do not replace seat belts, they only supplement them; adults in the back seat are not exempt, since they can be ticketed once the vehicle is stopped for another reason; opening the garage door does not make idling inside safe; carbon monoxide can kill before any symptom appears; anti-lock brakes are pressed steadily, never pumped.
Mnemonics: child seats step up by age two, four and eight — rear-facing, harness, then booster; stop within twenty-five feet at twenty miles per hour; idle no more than three minutes; the edge of a penny marks the thinnest legal tread.
Glossary: primary offense means a violation an officer can stop you for by itself; secondary law means a violation that can be ticketed only after a stop for another reason; ABS means an anti-lock braking system; SRS and SIR mean supplemental restraint system and supplemental inflatable restraint, the air bag markings; carbon monoxide means the odorless, colorless gas in vehicle exhaust; five-point harness means the harness the child passenger law requires in rear-facing and forward-facing child restraints.
Dynamic facts: fines, phone numbers and websites for child seat help, air bag switch requests and idling exemptions can change; confirm them on the official agency websites.
